implementation_notes: gMock, bundled with GoogleTest, generates the double from MOCK_METHOD declarations and stores the specification in EXPECT_CALL macros: argument matchers, Times() cardinality, InSequence ordering, and WillOnce/WillRepeatedly side effects and return values; a deviating call fails immediately and unfulfilled expectations fail when the mock is destroyed. The language has no reflection, so a framework or code generator is what makes mocks practical - the hand-written mock class is only justified where adding GoogleTest to the build is unacceptable.
pitfalls: EXPECT_CALL must be issued before the mock is handed to the code under test - alternating expectations and calls is undefined behaviour, so expectations read as future tense.
The mock must be destroyed while verification is still active; mocks allocated with new and never deleted skip final verification unless the heap checker is enabled.
Non-virtual and static members and final classes cannot be mocked by subclassing; they need the high-performance templates, a wrapper interface, or they stay real.

variants.name: Trompeloeil header-only mock
variants.implementation_notes: Trompeloeil is a header-only, thread-safe C++14 framework with a permissive licence: MAKE_MOCK declares the mocked members, REQUIRE_CALL and FORBID_CALL state expected and forbidden calls, sequence objects constrain order across several mocks, and cardinality is expressed with TIMES(AT_LEAST(1))-style limits. Choose it when the gMock dependency or licence is the blocker, or when the same mock must be reused across test frameworks through its adapters.
pitfalls: Expectations are checked when the mock is destroyed or when a verifying reporter runs; a mock kept alive in a fixture past the test silently defers the check.
The framework needs C++14 while newer coroutine helpers need C++20, so a mixed-standard project can trip on the include before any test runs.
